headline: After a Democratic Wave, the 2028 Field Waits on Newsom, Harris and Ocasio-Cortez
summary: Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress on November 3. A week later a handful of races were still uncalled, but the party had flipped at least seven Senate seats and built its largest House majority in years. Governors Josh Shapiro and JB Pritzker both won re-election, and Sen. Jon Ossoff won a second term in Georgia. Nobody has formally declared for 2028 yet.

The next few weeks are about decisions. Gov. Gavin Newsom told Turkey's Anadolu news agency on November 12 that he will decide in early January, and he has said he would not run if Kamala Harris does. Harris says she has not decided. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has said she would choose after the midterms between a presidential bid and a Senate run, and Rep. Ro Khanna says he will decide with his family after the holidays.

This is our first edition, so every number below is a starting estimate rather than a move. Harris leads national polling averages, while prediction markets favor Ossoff, who has said repeatedly that he will not run. We take him mostly at his word and rate him well below his market price. With no declared candidates and the first contest 14 months away, we keep 18 percent on someone not listed here.

headline: Denver Conference Previews the 2028 Field as Shapiro Steps Forward and Van Hollen Steps Aside
summary: Ten days after the midterms, would-be 2028 candidates tested their messages at the What's Next conference in Denver on November 13. Gov. Josh Shapiro, whom CNN describes as expected to run, gave a campaign-style speech and said he would be doing his part. Sen. Elissa Slotkin said she is seriously considering a run, Sen. Cory Booker said he is giving it hard thought, and Rep. Ro Khanna said the reception made him more likely to consider it. Nobody has formally declared.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who had previously expressed interest in a presidential run, told reporters he is not running in 2028 and is instead challenging Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leader in a December 1 vote. Pete Buttigieg said he would have no news on 2028 anytime soon, and Sen. Ruben Gallego said his three young children weigh heavily on his decision.

Odds moves are small this week. Shapiro rises a point on his post-election momentum, and Gallego slips a point. We add Booker and Slotkin to the board, moving their chances out of the unlisted field, which falls from 18 to 15 percent. Ossoff won a straw poll of 990 activists at Crooked Media's conference on November 7 and still leads prediction markets near 27 percent, but he says he is not running, so we hold him at 8. A CNN/SSRS poll taken before the midterms found Democrats about equally excited by Harris, Ocasio-Cortez and Buttigieg.

headline: DNC Schedules 12 Debates With a Dark-Money Pledge as Ossoff Tops a National Poll Despite Saying He Won't Run
summary: The Democratic National Committee set the rules of the road for 2028 on November 23. It will hold 12 primary debates, five in 2027, the first two in June and July, and seven in 2028, six of them in the early-voting states. Debates may be split across two nights with no more than 20 qualifying candidates, chosen by polling and grassroots fundraising. Candidates must also sign a pledge to denounce super PAC and dark-money spending that boosts them or attacks a Democratic rival, a largely symbolic rule the party cannot force outside groups to obey. Dates and media partners for the first two debates will be announced in January.

Nobody declared this week, but the groundwork continued. Allies of Pete Buttigieg launched Team Pete PAC to urge him to run, Cory Booker made his fourth South Carolina trip of the year and told reporters he is giving a run a lot of thought, and Gavin Newsom spent several days in Washington pitching AI regulation as an issue no 2028 candidate can ignore. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez filed paperwork for a House re-election bid, which does not settle her choice, and said Democrats should focus on getting results. Sen. Bernie Sanders, 85, said he probably will not run.

An Emerson College poll taken November 14 to 16 put Jon Ossoff first among Democratic primary voters at 17 percent, narrowly ahead of Kamala Harris at 16, Ocasio-Cortez at 15 and Buttigieg at 14, with Newsom at 11. Ossoff still says he is not running, so we hold him at 8. Odds moves are small: Booker rises a point to 3 on his South Carolina push, and Newsom slips a point to 11 as his polling has fallen from the mid-20s early this year to the low teens. The unlisted field holds at 15 percent.
